'''Edward Fulton Denison''' (December 18, 1915, [[Omaha]] – October 23, 1992, [[Washington D.C.]]) was an American economist.<ref name="nyt">{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/10/24/us/e-f-denison-economist-76-devised-gnp.html|title=E. F. Denison, Economist, 76; Devised G.N.P.|journal=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 24, 1992|first=Bruce|last=Lambert}}.</ref><ref name="wp">{{citation|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-1031437.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121105064916/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-1031437.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=November 5, 2012|title=Brookings Institution Economist Edward F. Denison Dies at 77|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|via=[[HighBeam Research]]|url-access=subscription|date=October 24, 1992}}.</ref><ref name="roiw">{{citation|url=http://www.roiw.org/1993/117.pdf|title=In Memoriam: Edward F. Denison, 1915–1992|journal=Review of Income and Wealth|volume=39|issue=1|year=1993|pages=117–119|first=John W.|last=Kendrick|authorlink=John Whitefield Kendrick|doi=10.1111/j.1475-4991.1993.tb00442.x}}.</ref> He was a pioneer in the measurement of the United States [[gross national product]]<ref name="nyt"/> and one of the founders of [[growth accounting]].<ref name="roiw"/>

Denison earned a bachelor's degree in economics in [[Oberlin College]] in 1936, a master's degree in [[Brown University]] in 1938, and a doctorate from Brown in 1941.<ref name="nyt"/> In 1948, he became acting chief of the National Income Division of the [[Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce]].<ref name="roiw"/> The next year, Edward also acted as assistant director and Chief Economist of the [[Office of Business Economics]].<ref name="nyt"/><ref name="roiw"/> In 1956 he left OBE to work for the [[Committee for Economic Development]].<ref name="roiw"/> From 1963, he served as a senior member of the [[Brookings Institution]] on economic research.<ref name="nyt"/><ref name="roiw"/>

In 1966 Denison was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]].<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm View/Search Fellows of the ASA] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/https://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, accessed 2016-08-20.</ref>
He became a distinguished fellow of the [[American Economic Association]] in 1981.<ref>[http://www.aeaweb.org/honors_awards/disting_fellows.php Distinguished fellows],  [[American Economic Association]], retrieved 2010-12-30.</ref>

He married Elsie Lightbown. His daughter, [[Janet Howell]], served in the Virginia Senate 1992–2024.<ref>{{cite news |work=The New York Times |accessdate=2011-06-05 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/10/24/us/e-f-denison-economist-76-devised-gnp.html |title=E. F. Denison, Economist, 76; Devised G.N.P. |date=October 24, 1992 |first=Bruce |last=Lambert}}</ref>

==Selected works==
*''Trends in American economic growth, 1929-1982'' (1962), published on ''[[The Journal of Business]]''
*''The Residual Factor and Economic Growth'' ([[Paris]], 1962)
*''The Sources of Economic Growth in the United States & the Alternatives Before us'' ([[New York City]], 1962), one that describes his theory mostly
*''Why growth rates differ; postwar experience in nine western countries'' ([[Washington D. C.]], 1967)
*''Accounting for United States economic growth, 1929-1969'' (Washington D. C., 1974)
*''Accounting for slower economic growth : the United States in the 1970s'' (Washington D. C., 1979)
